subtitle: Practice clarifying a decision and who owns it, building an options brief that shows who benefits and who bears the cost, raising uncomfortable risks across a power difference, and explaining a decision back so its effects can be learned from.
audience: For program leads, policy staff, supervisors and managers who prepare options and recommendations for someone else's decision, in disability services and across the agency. Useful whether you advise a director, a deputy director or a partner group.

lessons.title: The adviser's role: advising is not deciding
objectives: Clarify the decision, the decision owner and the deadline before beginning any analysis.
Distinguish advising on a decision from making it, including how an adviser can overstep or hold back.
Identify the parts of a request that belong with legal counsel, Human Resources or another responsible area.
Describe how your own defaults shape the way a question is framed to you and by you.
lessons.teaching:
Program leads, policy staff and managers may prepare recommendations for a director, deputy director, county partner or advisory group. Before substantial analysis begins, clarify the decision, the person or body authorized to make it, and the deadline. A request to look into a problem could concern a rule change, a process improvement or an explanation of existing practice. Those questions may require different evidence and different participants.

The Annie E. Casey Foundation's explanation of Person-Role-System asks leaders to examine how their experiences and roles influence their work. Its discussion of boundaries of authority, role and task offers a way to clarify a contribution and what is needed from others. In this course, apply that idea by discussing the scope of an advising assignment rather than assuming a job title answers every authority question. Identify what you can analyze or recommend, what you can decide and what requires another person's action.

Restate the request as a decision question and ask who must be consulted. Identify legal, employment, complaint or other specialist issues early, then use the applicable process with legal counsel, Human Resources, labor relations or Equal Opportunity and Access. These offices do not take over every responsibility held by management or staff. Confirm the deadline, any required action and the consequences of delay. Ask how the advice should be presented, including an accessible format, and send a short account back for correction or confirmation.

An adviser should explain the reasons for recommending one option and the evidence that supports it. Do not conceal a viable alternative merely because you prefer another, and identify options that cannot meet applicable requirements rather than presenting them as freely available choices. Likewise, withholding a material concern because someone else decides can leave the analysis incomplete. Clarifying authority supports useful advice while preserving required reporting and review.

Examine the assumptions in the question itself: whose problem it describes, whose experience is missing and what you have treated as relevant evidence. The Person-Role-System approach recognizes that personal and professional experiences influence how people occupy roles. Use that reflection to identify questions you should ask, not to infer another person's views from their background. Explain both what you know and what still needs to be learned before the decision.
lessons.keyPoint: Before you analyze anything, agree on the decision, the person who makes it and the deadline. Your job is to advise fully and honestly; the choice stays with the decision owner.
lessons.example: Practice case: Desmond, a deputy director in disability services who reads briefings with a screen reader, stops Rosa, a waiver policy lead, after a meeting. He asks her to look into how provider requests for rate exceptions are reviewed, because two lead agencies have complained about delays. He mentions that questions may come from above soon. Rosa has a full week ahead and is not sure whether he wants a process fix, a rule change or a talking point.
lessons.question: What should Rosa do first?
choices: Start pulling review-time data for every exception request this year, so she has useful evidence ready for whatever question he turns out to have.
Draft her own recommended fix for the delays and send it by Friday, since he asked for her judgment rather than for more questions.
Send Desmond three lines restating the decision, its deadline and who else is involved, ask how he wants the advice, and ask him to correct it.
feedback: Data will help later, but without knowing the decision Rosa may spend the week on the wrong question. Review times alone also say little about who waits longest and why.
A quick recommendation looks responsive, but it settles the question for Desmond and may answer something he did not ask. He would lose real options.
This is the recommended response. A few minutes of clarifying protects both roles: Desmond keeps the decision, and Rosa knows what evidence and which people her advice needs.
lessons.reflection: When someone senior asks you to look into something, what do you usually assume they mean? Where did you learn to make that assumption?
lessons.action: Pick one request you are working on for someone else's decision. Write two or three lines naming the decision, the person who makes it and the deadline, and ask that person to confirm or correct them.

check.question: What best separates an adviser's role from the decision owner's role?
check.correct: The adviser analyzes and recommends openly; the owner keeps the right to choose among real options.
wrong: The adviser settles the technical details, and the owner approves the final summary at the very end.
The adviser sets out the options evenly and leaves out a view, so the owner weighs them fresh.
check.feedback: Good advice includes a clear recommendation, but it keeps real options open. Narrowing the choice quietly is deciding; withholding a view leaves the owner without what you know. Both step outside the role.

lessons.title: Preparing an options brief that shows the tradeoffs
objectives: Prepare an options brief that includes no change, a minimum change and at least one fuller option.
State the evidence behind each option and where that evidence runs out.
Identify who benefits and who bears the cost of each option, using the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Tool questions.
Compare a Minimization, an Acceptance and an Adaptation habit in how an options brief is built.
lessons.teaching:
An options brief compares alternatives and explains the evidence for a recommendation. HM Treasury's Green Book retains business as usual as a comparison baseline and describes a minimum option that meets the proposal's objectives. This is United Kingdom guidance, used here as a method rather than Minnesota policy. Compare continued arrangements, a minimum option and fuller alternatives while checking applicable authority and requirements. A no-change baseline can show consequences even when it is not a lawful or viable choice. Identify that limit rather than presenting every comparison as an available decision.

For each option, state the evidence, uncertainty and effects that cannot be expressed as a number. The Green Book addresses these distinctions in presenting an appraisal. Minnesota's Equity Analysis Tool asks how data were separated by characteristics such as race, gender, disability and income, and what the findings show. The Annie E. Casey Foundation's Action Guide warns against relying only on available data without asking what information is needed. Explain the gap without treating missing evidence as evidence that no difference exists.

Examine where benefits, costs and additional work may fall. The Minnesota tool asks about affected groups and access, including disability, language and culture. GARE's toolkit asks about benefits, burdens and unintended consequences. Include effects outside the agency, such as additional work for counties, costs to providers or barriers for people receiving services. Distinguish a reported experience from a verified pattern, and say when people affected have not yet been heard. Do not dismiss a report merely because it cannot establish how common the problem is.

The following program illustrations use IDI, LLC's continuum vocabulary to examine assumptions in a brief; they do not assess anyone's orientation. A Minimization habit may emphasize a single average while overlooking differences in experience. An Acceptance habit examines those differences and the categories used in the analysis. An Adaptation habit changes the method, such as asking affected people to check an account of costs or considering an alternative they propose. No individual speaks for everyone in a group. Provide an accessible way to contribute, identify remaining uncertainty and give your recommendation with its reasons.
lessons.keyPoint: Show real options, including no change and the smallest workable change. For each one, say what the evidence shows, where it runs out, who gains and who carries the cost.
lessons.example: Practice case: Joanne, a division director in disability services, has asked Hamid, a program consultant, for options on how lead agency case managers will be trained on a new assessment. The cheapest option moves every session online and saves travel money. On a call, Esther, a lead agency supervisor, tells Hamid that some small agencies share one meeting room with poor internet, and that two case managers who are Deaf need interpreters booked well ahead. The brief is due tomorrow.
lessons.question: How should Hamid finish the brief?
choices: Keep all three options, add a line to each on who gains and who bears the cost, and note Esther's points and what is unchecked.
Drop the online option from the brief, since he now knows it would shut out some case managers and Joanne should not be offered it.
Keep the brief as drafted and mention Esther's points to Joanne in person, since one supervisor's account is not yet firm evidence.
feedback: Joanne sees the alternatives, reported access concerns and remaining checks. The brief should identify the supports and legal or policy review needed before treating an option as viable.

An online option with effective interpretation and connection support may remain viable after the relevant checks. An option that cannot meet applicable requirements should be identified as infeasible, with the reason recorded.
Caution about one account is sensible, but leaving it out of the written brief means the risk can vanish from the record. Hamid can label it as one report still to be confirmed.
lessons.reflection: When you write about the people an option affects, whom do you picture first? Whose situation do you find yourself filling in by guessing?
lessons.action: Take one option in a brief or proposal you are working on and write a single line for it: who gains, who carries the cost or extra work, and how you know. Note one group you have not yet heard from.

check.question: What does a benefit and burden line add to each option in a brief?
check.correct: It shows where each option's costs and extra work land, and what that claim rests on.
wrong: It shows which groups the analysis covered, so the brief can show it was checked.
It shows each option's total benefit to people served, so the options can be ranked.
check.feedback: A brief can be accurate on totals and still hide where the cost lands. The benefit and burden line makes the tradeoff visible, including costs that move onto partners, families or people receiving services.

lessons.title: Saying the uncomfortable part across a power difference
objectives: State a risk or a missing perspective to the decision owner early, plainly and with its evidence.
Explain how a power difference and different norms about disagreement can keep advice quiet.
Write a risk into a brief so it travels with the decision.
Route concerns about law, labor agreements or discrimination to legal counsel, labor relations or the equal opportunity office.
lessons.teaching:
An adviser may need to raise a risk that challenges a preferred option, a timetable or an announced plan. HM Treasury's Green Book calls for objective, honest and impartial advice in its United Kingdom setting. In this course, that principle means distinguishing the evidence you have, the interpretation you offer and the questions that remain unresolved. Omitting a concern from a brief does not resolve its possible effects.

A power difference may affect how someone raises disagreement, particularly when the decision maker influences assignments or performance reviews. Communication habits also vary within families, workplaces and cultures. Neither appearance nor silence establishes a person's expectations or whether they understood your concern. Ask how to provide the information clearly and check what still needs discussion, without requiring personal disclosure.

Raise the risk as relevant information, with its evidence and limits. Ask for a conversation before the brief is final when the situation allows. State the concern, who may bear its effects, what remains uncertain and what review or information is needed. The Government Alliance on Race and Equity offers brief questions about racial equity impacts, benefits and burdens, and reducing unintended consequences. Use such questions to support inquiry rather than treating a quick discussion as a substitute for necessary analysis. Record material risks through the appropriate channels so they remain available for review.

For ordinary choices within the decision maker's lawful authority, distinguish your recommendation from their decision. That distinction does not cancel required reporting, protected disclosures or an applicable review process. Flag possible conflicts with law, rules or labor agreements and seek the appropriate legal or labor-relations review. Follow designated procedures for possible discrimination, harassment or retaliation, including supervisors' additional reporting duties. Do not wait to prove a violation through an independent inquiry.

If asked to remove a material risk, explain why it matters and seek an appropriate way to preserve an accurate record. An unresolved concern may warrant an authorized reporting or escalation route. Minnesota Statutes section 181.932 protects specified employee reports and disclosures, subject to its conditions, while retaining limits on disclosing protected data. This course cannot determine whether a particular report qualifies for legal protection.
lessons.keyPoint: Raise risks early with their evidence and record them through appropriate channels. Clarify decision authority while following required reporting, review and escalation procedures. Protect information that cannot lawfully be disclosed.
lessons.example: Practice case: Adaeze, a manager in a benefits processing area, has asked Tomasz, a supervisor, to finish a brief supporting her plan to end evening phone hours and move staff to daytime shifts. She has already mentioned the plan to her director. Tomasz's team knows that evening callers are mostly people who work during the day, and that many of them use an interpreter. Nobody has asked callers or the evening staff, and moving staff to daytime shifts would also need labor relations to review it. The brief is due Thursday, and Adaeze wants it short.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz do?
choices: Write the short brief she asked for, then raise the evening callers with her once the change starts and its effects can be measured.
Ask Adaeze for fifteen minutes before Thursday, explain who uses evening hours, and put that risk and the missing voices in the brief.
Raise the concern with her director directly, since the plan is already moving and the director can still change its course.
feedback: Respecting her request is reasonable, but waiting means callers who work days bear the cost first, and Adaeze decides without what Tomasz's team already knows.
This raises the operational risk before the decision and records the missing perspectives. Tomasz should also flag the need for labor-relations review; a short brief does not remove that requirement.

In this scenario, Adaeze has not yet heard the concern, so discussing it with her is a reasonable first step. This is not a rule against contacting another authorized person: urgent risks, reporting duties, protected disclosures or unresolved concerns may warrant another route.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time you held back advice from someone senior. What did you weigh, and what did you learn early in life or work about disagreeing upward?
lessons.action: Before your next brief goes out, add a short section on risks and missing perspectives. Write one sentence for each, with its evidence, and share it with the decision owner before the brief is final.

check.question: Your manager has announced a preferred option. You identify an ordinary operational risk, with no separate reporting or escalation requirement. What is the adviser's next step?
check.correct: Raise the risk early with its evidence, put it in the brief and leave the choice to her.
wrong: Raise the risk with her in conversation, but keep the written brief to what she asked for.
Put the risk in the brief, then raise it with her director so the concern is heard in time.
check.feedback: For the ordinary operational risk described here, raise the evidence with the decision maker and include it in the brief. The answer does not waive legal or policy requirements, authorized escalation or protected reporting rights.

lessons.title: After the decision: explaining it and learning from it
objectives: Explain a decision to the people affected, including its reasons and who bears its costs.
Distinguish explaining a decision from defending it or distancing yourself from it.
Plan two or three group-level signals that will show whether a decision worked and for whom.
Describe how to bring results back to the decision owner as plainly as the original advice.
lessons.teaching:
Explaining a decision is part of implementation, alongside the work needed to carry it out and respond to its effects. An adviser may be asked to explain the decision to staff, partners, providers or people receiving services. The Government Alliance on Race and Equity toolkit includes communication and accountability, while Minnesota's Equity Analysis Tool asks how partners will remain informed and involved. An explanation gives people information they can use to plan, ask questions and raise concerns; it does not guarantee trust or agreement.

Describe what changed, when it takes effect and the reasons for choosing it over alternatives. Identify the costs and tradeoffs without minimizing them, and distinguish the adopted decision from your own recommendation. You can acknowledge relevant disagreement without replacing the explanation with a defense of your position. Explain what remains unchanged and identify applicable complaint, appeal or reporting routes. Use accessible documents, interpretation or translation as needed, and provide an opportunity for questions.

Plan evaluation before implementation rather than waiting until someone asks whether the change worked. The Green Book addresses early evaluation planning and the distribution of effects across groups. Minnesota's Step-by-Step Guide calls for monitoring, adjustment and sharing lessons, and the Annie E. Casey Foundation's Action Guide describes continuing evaluation. For the exercise, choose a small set of indicators, identify who will review them and agree when findings will be reported. State what each indicator can show and what would require additional evidence.

Use aggregate indicators for this learning exercise and keep identifying details about staff or people receiving services out of your notes. This does not prohibit authorized program evaluation or required individual records. Before using operational data, confirm the purpose, authority, access rules and safeguards with the responsible area. Section 13.05 limits collection, use and disclosure of data on individuals. Small groups, combined details or quotations may still identify someone, so a group label alone does not establish that information is safe to share.

Bring findings to the decision maker with their limitations: what changed, for whom, what remains uncertain and what you recommend keeping, changing or stopping. Explain how people can raise continuing concerns without requiring them to agree with the decision. Individual service, eligibility and licensing decisions remain subject to their authorized processes.
lessons.keyPoint: Explain the decision, reasons, costs and available routes for questions or concerns. Agree how to assess its effects using authorized information, appropriate privacy safeguards and clear limits on what the findings show.
lessons.example: Practice case: Disability services has decided to move travel reimbursement for members of a self-advocate advisory group from same-day payment to a monthly process. Mei-Ling, the program lead who advised on it, recommended keeping same-day payment for members who asked for it. The deputy director chose a single monthly process. Jerome, the group's co-chair, has given Mei-Ling fifteen minutes at the next meeting. Several members rely on the payment to cover their rides.
lessons.question: How should Mei-Ling use her fifteen minutes?
choices: Tell members she argued for keeping same-day payment, so they know she was on their side, and suggest they write to the deputy director.
Present the change briefly as an administrative update, so the meeting can move on to the agenda items members care about most.
Explain what changed, why, who bears the cost and what stays the same, then agree with members how they will report how it is working.
feedback: Mentioning her recommendation may be relevant, but it does not replace an explanation of the adopted decision, its reasons and effects. Members should also receive information about applicable ways to raise concerns or seek review.
A short update respects the agenda, but it hides a real cost for members who rely on the payment for rides, and it gives no way to learn whether the change works.
This is the recommended response. Members get an accurate account, including the cost, and a way to report effects that Mei-Ling can bring back to the deputy director.
lessons.reflection: When a decision you disagreed with was explained to you, what helped you trust the explanation, and what made you doubt it?
lessons.action: For a decision you are advising on now, write one page: the decision and its owner, the real options, who benefits and who bears the cost of each, what is missing, and how you will learn whether it worked.

check.question: After a decision you advised against, what is your task when explaining it to the people affected?
check.correct: Explain it accurately, costs included, and set up a way to learn how it works.
wrong: Explain that you argued against it, so people know who is responsible for the outcome.
Explain the change and its benefits briefly, and take questions about costs one to one afterward.
check.feedback: Explain the adopted decision accurately, including costs, uncertainty and applicable routes for concerns or review. Learning from its effects requires appropriate follow-through; an explanation does not guarantee trust or agreement.

cards.back: The person or body with the authority to make a particular choice. Advisers analyze and recommend; the decision owner chooses and is accountable for the choice.
A short written comparison of realistic choices for one decision, with the evidence for each, its limits, who benefits, who bears the cost and the adviser's labeled recommendation.
What happens if nothing changes. HM Treasury's Green Book always carries it into the detailed comparison as the benchmark the other options are measured against.
Who gains from an option and who carries its cost or extra work, including costs that move onto partners, families or people receiving services.
An agreement, made before a change begins, on which group-level signals will show whether it worked, for whom, when you will look and who will hear the results.

aid.heading: Before you start the analysis
items: Restate the request as a decision question with a choice in it.
Confirm who decides, who must be consulted and the deadline.
Ask how the decision owner wants advice, including an accessible format.
Name any part that belongs with legal counsel, Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office.
Ask who is affected and whose experience is missing from the question.

aid.heading: Building and delivering the options brief
items: Include no change, the smallest workable change and one or two fuller options.
For each option, state the evidence and where it runs out.
Write one line per option: who gains, who carries the cost and how you know.
Put risks and missing perspectives in writing, and raise them early in person.
Label your recommendation as yours and give your reasons.

aid.heading: After the decision
items: Explain what changed, why, who bears the cost and what stays the same.
Offer the explanation in plain language and forms people can use.
Agree on two or three group-level signals and when you will look.
Bring results back to the decision owner: keep, change or stop.
Use authorized data and suitable privacy safeguards; keep identifying details out of this learning exercise.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide (June 2024)
sources.note: Supports the course's use of the tool's questions on groups positively or negatively affected, disaggregated data, access and accessibility, and keeping partners informed. Check agency rules on when its use is required.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Step-by-Step Guide: Applying the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Tool (June 2024)
sources.note: Supports lesson 4's steps on monitoring progress, adjusting based on evaluation and feedback, and reflecting on and sharing lessons learned. A companion to the Quick Guide, not a rule.

sources.title: HM Treasury — The Green Book: Appraisal and Evaluation in Central Government (2026)
sources.note: Adapted from its guidance on business as usual and do minimum options, stating uncertainty, who bears costs, honest advice, explaining the choice and early evaluation plans. United Kingdom central government; used for method only.

sources.title: Government Alliance on Race and Equity — Racial Equity Toolkit: An Opportunity to Operationalize Equity (2015, updated 2016)
sources.note: Supports the benefit and burden and unintended consequences questions, the three quick questions for fast decisions, and communication and accountability as a step. Written for United States local government.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation — Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide (2014)
sources.note: Supports the caution about using available rather than needed data and the cycle of implementing, tracking, assessing and revising. Written for foundations and partner organizations; race-specific by design.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation — Get Results by Understanding Person-Role-System
sources.note: Supports the explanation of personal experience and roles, and boundaries of authority, role and task. The advising steps are program applications of that framework, not a grant of legal or organizational authority.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the continuum terms used in lesson 2: Minimization stressing commonality that can hide difference, Acceptance and Adaptation. Used to describe habits in building a brief; no one is assessed.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes — Section 181.932, Disclosure of Information by Employees
sources.note: Supports the distinction between ordinary advice and specified protected employee reports or disclosures, subject to statutory conditions and limits on disclosing protected data.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes — Section 13.05, Duties of Responsible Authority
sources.note: Supports limits on collection, storage, use and dissemination of data on individuals. The learning exercise does not authorize access or disclosure.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
sources.note: Supports agency complaint reporting and supervisors' additional referral duties. Confirm current contacts and procedures on the DHS intranet.
